title: Karna's abandonment
hook: a son is born shining, in armor and earrings, and his young mother sets him on the river
carry: a person on each side of it

segments.voice: Yesterday, Karna's abandonment began: Pritha, Durvasa's mantra, and the sun answering a girl's curiosity. I only wanted to see if it worked.

A baby is born in secret, already dressed for battle. The Mahabharata says he's born wearing armor that's part of his own body, with bright earrings in his ears, shining like his father, the sun. Any newborn would be scandal enough for an unmarried girl in a king's house. This one glows. There's no hiding him in a corner. And his mother is still very young, still a daughter under her father's roof.
screen: `BORN IN SECRET.` → `ARMOR AND EARRINGS.` → `SHINING LIKE THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Kunti's choice is quick in the telling, and heavy in the hearing. Afraid of what her family and the world will say, she places her newborn son in a basket and sets it on the river. A later part of the poem tells the scene again at length: she weeps over the basket and speaks to the child, asking the gods of the waters, the sky and the earth to keep him safe, and saying that whoever finds him will be blessed to raise him. Then the current carries him away. Listen to the word the text chooses. It doesn't call her cruel. It calls her afraid, tells us why, and lets us watch her grief. Some readers hear a mother failing her child. Some hear a frightened girl doing the only thing she could see to do. Some hear both at once, and the poem seems to allow that. And notice the armor. The baby is sent off alone, but not unprotected. He's wrapped in his father's gift, and those earrings and that armor will matter enormously later. The word abandonment can sound like a verdict. In this story, it's also an event with a person on each side of it: a mother on the bank, a child on the water. The Mahabharata will follow both of them for a very long time.
screen: `SHE SETS HIM ON THE RIVER.` · `THE TEXT SAYS: AFRAID.` · `A FAILURE, A FEAR, OR BOTH?` · `WRAPPED IN HIS FATHER'S GIFT.` · then, large: `A PERSON ON EACH SIDE.`

segments.voice: This one is tender, so go slowly. Let one decision come to mind that someone made about you before you could have a say, and see that there was a person on the other side, deciding. Then notice what went with you anyway, the way the armor went with the child: something that kept you.
Karna's abandonment. A son born shining in armor and earrings, set adrift by a frightened mother who blessed him as he went.
Your line: a person on each side of it. Downstream, someone is waiting. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some retellings of the Mahabharata, in storytelling, dance and theater, linger on Kunti at the riverbank, letting audiences sit with her grief rather than rushing past it.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (birth of Kunti's son with armor and earrings; he is set on the water)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm that the Adi Parva gives Kunti's fear of her relatives/the world as the reason, and that the Vana Parva (Kundalaharana) retells the scene with her lament invoking the gods of water, sky and earth.
Confirm 'basket' (Ganguli may say basket or box/chest); the river's name is deliberately left out.
The 'some readers' views are the script's framing, given without ranking.
